papers.title: Automated Sleep Staging Performance Across Two Experimental Sleep Manipulation Protocols in Adolescents.
papers.abstract: Automated sleep staging algorithms improve the scalability of polysomnography analysis in adolescent research but are primarily validated in undisturbed, single-night sleep recordings. It remains unclear whether these algorithms maintain performance when sleep architecture is experimentally manipulated. This study evaluated the validity of two popular automated sleep staging approaches across two distinct sleep manipulation paradigms in adolescents: a sleep restriction protocol (N=43, mean age [SD]=13.37[1.06] years; four nights including two sleep extension [10hr] and two restriction [4hr] nights) and a slow-wave sleep deprivation (SWSD) protocol (N=18, mean age [SD]=17.17[1.79] years; baseline, SWSD, and recovery nights). Automated sleep staging was performed using the POPulation-level Sleep Stager (POPS), the Yet Another Spindle Algorithm (YASA), and combined POPS+YASA. Manual polysomnography scoring by experienced sleep technicians served as the reference standard. Agreement was assessed using Cohen's k, and stage-specific performance was evaluated using F1 scores and confusion matrices. Mixed-effects models tested differences in overall and stage-specific agreement across nights. All staging approaches demonstrated moderate-to-substantial agreement with manual scoring across manipulated sleep conditions (k range; range=0.53-0.76). In the sleep restriction study, agreement was lower in restricted versus extended sleep (P<0.05), and agreement declined across restriction nights, with poorer Wake, N1, and N2 classification, while N3 remained preserved. In the SWSD study, overall agreement was lower on the SWSD night, with poorer N3 classification while other stages were preserved. Automated sleep staging performance may be less consistent in adolescents when sleep is curtailed or fragmented; future studies should develop and validate these algorithms under multiple sleep conditions.

papers.title: Evaluating Bayesian deep learning for robust biomedical time-series classification under distribution shift: A sleep scoring case study
papers.abstract: In biomedical time-series classification, machine learning models often suffer from deteriorating accuracy and calibration due to distribution shift. We investigate to what degree Bayesian-inspired deep learning improves robustness through Bayesian model averaging (BMA). Using rodent sleep scoring as a case study, we evaluate BMA under distribution shifts in genotype, laboratory, and species. We systematically compare nine approximate inference methods spanning single- and multi-basin approaches across two neural network backbones on in-distribution (ID) data and five out-of-distribution (OOD) datasets. In our results, multi-basin methods perform best, outperforming baselines and single-basin methods. Compared with point estimates, BMA generally improves OOD accuracy and calibration across both architectures, while yielding only modest ID gains. It also often improves selective prediction and OOD and artifact detection, but, interestingly, not inter-rater disagreement detection.

papers.title: A Unified Flexible Large Polysomnography Model for Sleep Staging and Downstream Clinical Screening
papers.abstract: Polysomnography (PSG) is central to sleep medicine, yet its analysis remains hindered by labor-intensive manual scoring and limited cross-center generalizability. We present LPSGM, a large-scale PSG model trained on 220,500 hours of data from 16 public datasets (24,000 recordings) that addresses two challenges: cross-center sleep staging generalization and PSG-based screening of narcolepsy, obstructive sleep apnea (OSA), and depression. LPSGM integrates domain-adaptive pre-training, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture to accommodate heterogeneous recording protocols. In prospective validation, LPSGM achieves expert-level sleep staging ({kappa} = 0.845 {+/-} 0.066 vs. inter-expert {kappa} = 0.850 {+/-} 0.102) and matches fully supervised models on independent private cohorts. For downstream screening, LPSGM achieves 84.2% accuracy ({kappa} = 0.761) in three-class narcolepsy classification, with cross-institutional transfer for normal-versus-abnormal hypersomnia yielding an AUC of 0.879. Severe OSA screening reaches an AUC of 0.874 without access to respiratory signals. Depression symptom screening achieves an AUC of 0.801 in a surrogate-labeled APPLES cohort, and cross-dataset transfer to an independent clinically diagnosed cohort reaches an AUC of 0.965. These results suggest that LPSGM's pre-trained representations capture sleep-related signatures that generalize across institutions and support PSG-based screening of clinically relevant conditions. The code and pre-trained model are publicly available at https://github.com/Deng-GuiFeng/LPSGM.

ai.summary: Presents LPSGM, a large PSG model trained on 220,500 hours from 16 public datasets, integrating domain-adaptive pretraining, flexible channel configurations, and a unified architecture for cross-center sleep staging and clinical screening. It achieved expert-level staging (kappa 0.845 vs inter-expert 0.850) and supported narcolepsy, OSA, and depression screening with AUCs up to 0.965 in transfer cohorts.

papers.title: RefineSleepNet: Task-Driven Signal-Domain Transformation for EEG/EOG Sleep Staging.
papers.abstract: Automatic sleep staging relies on effective representation of physiological signals. Representative raw-signal sleep-staging encoders typically transform input waveforms while progressively compressing their temporal resolution within the same encoding path. However, explicit modality-specific, sample-aligned, and task-driven signal-domain transformation before epoch-level feature extraction remains comparatively underexplored. To investigate this design, we propose RefineSleepNet, an end-to-end sequence-to-sequence framework that explicitly separates these two stages. Separately parameterized Signal Refinement U-Net (SRU-Net) branches first transform EEG and EOG waveforms while preserving the original temporal length, after which Epoch Feature Extractors (EFEs) extract epoch-level representations from the refined signals. Fused Sequence Attention (FSA) then performs multimodal integration and cross-epoch contextual modeling before epoch-wise classification. All stages are jointly optimized using the final sleep-staging objective without a separate waveform reconstruction target. RefineSleepNet was evaluated on Sleep-EDF-39, Sleep-EDF-153, and ISRUC-3 using subject-independent 10-fold cross-validation, achieving accuracy/macro-F1 (MF1) scores of 84.5%/79.8%, 83.5%/78.1%, and 80.3%/78.1%, respectively. Ablation experiments supported the coordinated design, while statistical analysis and intermediate-representation evaluations further examined the robustness and characteristics of the learned transformation. The learned transformation retained broad temporal and spectral organization while introducing local waveform changes and modality-specific spectral redistribution. These results support the staged organization as a viable modeling strategy for EEG/EOG sleep staging.

ai.summary: Proposes RefineSleepNet, a sequence-to-sequence framework that first applies separate Signal Refinement U-Net branches to EEG and EOG waveforms preserving temporal length, then extracts epoch features with fusion and cross-epoch attention. Under subject-independent 10-fold cross-validation it reached accuracy/macro-F1 of 84.5%/79.8% on Sleep-EDF-39, 83.5%/78.1% on Sleep-EDF-153, and 80.3%/78.1% on ISRUC-3.

papers.title: CSPT-SleepNet: An Automatic Sleep Staging Framework Integrating Center-Driven Sequence Supervision and Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoding.
papers.abstract: Background: Automatic sleep staging is fundamental to sleep architecture analysis and the diagnosis of sleep disorders. Sleep staging requires jointly modeling complementary information across modalities, multi-scale physiological features, and temporal relationships across consecutive epochs. In target epoch prediction from consecutive epochs, non-target epochs primarily provide contextual information, but their ground-truth labels remain underused as auxiliary supervision. Methods: We propose CSPT-SleepNet, an automatic sleep staging framework integrating center-driven sequence supervision with multimodal pyramid token encoding. A Multimodal Pyramid Token Encoder extracts hierarchical multi-scale features from electroencephalogram, electrooculogram, and electromyogram signals, followed by intra-modal, cross-modal, and inter-epoch modeling for center-epoch classification. During training, the center epoch receives primary classification supervision, while non-center epochs receive weaker auxiliary supervision based on their ground-truth labels, providing stage-informed contextual support for the prediction target. Results: In subject-independent cross-validation on Sleep-EDF-20, Sleep-EDF-78, and ISRUC-S3, CSPT-SleepNet achieved accuracy (ACC)/macro F1 (MF1) scores of 87.93%/83.53%, 85.81%/80.87%, and 84.06%/82.86%, respectively. In a separate controlled comparison on Sleep-EDF-20, center-driven sequence supervision improved ACC and MF1 by 0.60 and 0.91 percentage points, respectively, over equal-weight sequence supervision. The full model has 3.418 million trainable parameters and requires 397.10 million floating-point operations for an input sequence of nine 30-s epochs. Conclusions: CSPT-SleepNet provides an effective framework for center-epoch sleep staging from consecutive multimodal inputs. Nevertheless, N1 recognition remains challenging, with F1 scores ranging from 55.3% to 62.7% across the three datasets.

papers.title: Physiology-Informed Blink Artefact Detection from Bilateral Frontal EEG Under Asymmetric Interference.
papers.abstract: Eye blinks contaminate frontal electroencephalography (EEG), while asymmetric disturbances can cause false detections. We present a physiology-informed detector that combines waveform correlation, peak-time agreement, amplitude similarity, and symmetric-component dominance in an explicit event-verification rule. It uses two frontal channels without supervised model fitting. Evaluation on raw ZuCo 1.0 recordings included 260 eligible blocks from 12 participants, totalling 1291.61 min and 8611 eye-tracker reference intervals. Scalp and periocular pairs were evaluated separately. On the scalp pair, participant-mean precision was 0.731, recall 0.774, F1 0.734, and false positives 1.469 per minute. At fixed settings, false-positive rates were lower than with single-channel thresholding and bilateral averaging (both Holm-adjusted p = 0.005859), and remained lower than those of four rule-based controls across five perturbation conditions. Threshold-selected simple controls achieved higher precision at similar recall. Component ablations quantified the effects of the verification checks on sensitivity and false positives. The offline Python detector required a median of 2.13 ms per minute of recorded data on an Apple M1 Pro. These results establish a computationally inexpensive approach that makes blink-event decisions directly inspectable through bilateral signal measurements.

ai.reason: Lightweight, unsupervised, fast Python artifact detector using frontal channels; directly matches artifact-removal and CPU-friendly interests.
ai.summary: Develops a physiology-informed blink artifact detector for bilateral frontal EEG that combines waveform correlation, peak-time agreement, amplitude similarity, and symmetric-component dominance in an explicit rule without supervised model fitting. On ZuCo 1.0 scalp-pair data it achieved participant-mean precision 0.731, recall 0.774, and F1 0.734, with lower false-positive rates than single-channel thresholding and bilateral averaging.

papers.title: Agentic EEG Pipeline Synthesis Using Large Language Models and the Model Context Protocol.
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography analysis typically requires multistage processing pipelines for which configuration depends on recording characteristics and the intended analytical objective. Although automated pipelines improve reproducibility, they generally implement predefined processing sequences. We present an agentic framework in which a large language model (LLM) orchestrator synthesizes and executes task-specific EEG processing workflows by selecting, parameterizing, and ordering established signal processing components accessed through Model Context Protocol interfaces. Computational EEG processing and analysis operations are performed using established EEGLAB (version 2026.0.0) implementations running in MATLAB (R2026a), while structured execution results and quality control information are returned to the orchestrator to support adaptation during execution. The framework is evaluated by examining tool-layer execution fidelity, independent pipeline synthesis, and the quality of the resulting EEG output relative to the established DISCOVER-EEG workflow. In an evaluation using eight resting state EEG recordings from four participants, mean epoch retention was 0.845 for the agent-generated pipeline and 0.843 for DISCOVER-EEG, while mean spectral entropy was 4.87 and 4.84 bits, respectively. Mean signal-to-noise ratio was 13.92 dB for the agent-generated pipeline and 11.14 dB for DISCOVER-EEG; however, this difference should be interpreted cautiously because the pipelines used different upper filter boundaries. A secondary analysis examined whether EEG processed using the generated pipeline retained features relevant to Alzheimer's disease versus healthy control classification. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of coupling LLM-based orchestration with EEG processing software to generate executable task-specific workflows with structured execution records and provenance. Further evaluation across larger datasets, independent synthesis runs, and additional EEG paradigms is required in order to establish repeatability and generalizability.

ai.reason: Reproducible, GUI-adjacent automated EEG pipelines integrated with EEGLAB; strongly relevant to open-source software and reproducible analysis interests.
ai.summary: Presents an agentic framework in which an LLM orchestrator selects, parameterizes, and orders EEGLAB components via Model Context Protocol interfaces to synthesize task-specific EEG processing pipelines. On eight resting-state recordings, agent-generated pipelines achieved mean epoch retention 0.845 versus 0.843 for DISCOVER-EEG and mean SNR 13.92 dB versus 11.14 dB (interpreted cautiously due to differing filter boundaries).

papers.title: EOG Artifact Removal from EEG Using a Gated WGAN with Multi-Scale and Multi-Domain Feature Extraction.
papers.abstract: Background: Electroencephalogram (EEG) signals provide important information for brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) and the diagnosis of neurological disorders but are susceptible to electrooculographic (EOG) artifacts. Traditional methods often rely on multichannel data or relatively long windows, limiting online applicability. Deep learning enables single-channel end-to-end artifact removal, but existing methods may not fully exploit features in the time and frequency domains and may unnecessarily modify relatively clean EEG. Methods: We developed a Wasserstein generative adversarial network (WGAN) integrating reconstruction loss, multi-domain and multi-scale feature extraction, and a gating unit. Reconstruction loss improved waveform reconstruction, yielding a reconstruction-loss-assisted artifact-removal WGAN (rarWGAN). Parallel branches with different kernel sizes extracted multi-scale features, while a multi-domain module combined temporal features with spectral features extracted using complex-valued convolutions. Integrating both modules into rarWGAN produced MDS-rarWGAN. Based on discriminator scores, gating routed inputs classified as contaminated to the generator and retained the others unchanged. Results: On EEGdenoiseNet, MDS-rarWGAN yielded relative root mean square errors (RRMSEs) of 0.189 ± 0.028 and 0.183 ± 0.027 in the time and frequency domains, respectively, with a correlation coefficient of 0.955 ± 0.013. Compared with rarWGAN, RRMSEs decreased by 23.2% and 32.5%, respectively, and the correlation coefficient increased by 1.2%. The gating unit yielded false positive and false negative rates of 1.47% and 0.12%, respectively. For EEG containing artifacts, no statistically significant differences in time domain RRMSE were detected with and without gating (all p > 0.05). On BCI Competition IV 2a, reconstruction metrics measured agreement with a reference derived from independent component analysis (ICA), as artifact-free EEG ground truth was unavailable. Using the same EEGNet classifier, EEG processed by gated-MDS-rarWGAN achieved the highest mean motor imagery classification accuracy among the evaluated deep learning methods. Conclusions: The method suppresses EOG artifacts, reduces unnecessary processing of signals without evident artifacts, and supports motor imagery decoding, offering a feasible preprocessing approach.

ai.reason: Directly targets EEG artifact removal with single-channel end-to-end processing, relevant to the researcher's artifact-removal interest, though it is a heavier deep-learning system.
ai.summary: Develops a gated, reconstruction-loss-assisted Wasserstein GAN (MDS-rarWGAN) with multi-scale and multi-domain feature extraction for single-channel EOG artifact removal from EEG. On EEGdenoiseNet it reached RRMSEs of 0.189 (time) and 0.183 (frequency) with correlation 0.955, and gated processing yielded the highest mean motor imagery classification accuracy among evaluated deep learning methods on BCI Competition IV 2a.

papers.title: The electro-MICA toolbox for integrating electrophysiology within multimodal imaging and connectomics workflows.
papers.abstract: The integration of electrophysiological recordings with multimodal neuroimaging data holds great promise for advancing our understanding of brain function and neurological disorders. To facilitate this endeavor, we present electro-MICA, an open-access Python toolbox designed to project electrophysiological features from scalp and intracranial electroencephalography (EEG) onto cortical and hippocampal surfaces generated by validated multimodal imaging ecosystems. The toolbox comprises two pipelines: one for intracranial EEG (iEEG) recorded with stereo-EEG depth electrodes and one for scalp EEG source localization. Both pipelines are grounded in numerical solutions to the electromagnetic equations governing electric activity in the brain, solved using the Boundary Element Method. A key methodological contribution is the use of a current density double layer model for neural generators, which avoids the mathematical singularities introduced by conventional dipole-based models when electrodes are near the cortical surface, a situation that can arise in iEEG. Electrode contacts are additionally modeled with non-zero length, improving physical realism. Scalp EEG source localization is performed using eLORETA on a subject-specific three-layer head model derived from the anatomical input. Validation against empirical gamma-band iEEG data from 32 subjects demonstrates that the distributed generator model outperforms both distance-based and dipole-based alternatives. An illustrative clinical example demonstrates the toolbox's capacity to reveal associations between intracranial spike rates, cortical thickness, and anatomical connectivity in an epilepsy patient. Electro-MICA requires no parameter selection from the user, facilitating straightforward multimodal analyses. The toolbox is available at http://github.com/MICA-MNI/electromica with extensive online documentation at http://electromica.readthedocs.io.

ai.reason: Open-source Python toolbox for projecting EEG/iEEG to cortical surfaces; transferable source-localization and integration methods relevant to neural time-series workflows.
ai.summary: Introduces electro-MICA, an open-access Python toolbox that projects scalp and intracranial EEG features onto cortical and hippocampal surfaces using Boundary Element Method solutions, a current density double layer generator model, and eLORETA source localization. Validation against gamma-band iEEG from 32 subjects showed the distributed generator model outperformed distance-based and dipole-based alternatives.

papers.title: NOMAD-EEG: Native Omni-Montage Adaptive Diffusion
papers.abstract: Purpose. Electroencephalography (EEG) montages, channel counts and recording lengths vary widely, but most EEG foundation models are bound to the channel set and input length they were trained on. We aimed to build a generative EEG foundation model independent of the number, identity and order of electrodes and of the input length. Methods. NOMAD-EEG is a 12.0 M-parameter diffusion model that alternates state-space layers along time, without patches, with attention across electrodes identified only by their 3D scalp position. It was pre-trained on 147 h of unlabelled EEG from a single corpus and evaluated with frozen linear probes on ten datasets with 1 to 64 electrodes against seven foundation models run under one protocol, and on two unseen populations. Results. Despite its small size (12.0 M parameters against 69 M for REVE) and single pre- training corpus, NOMAD-EEG outperformed all seven foundation models on EEGMMIDB mo- tor imagery (balanced accuracy 0.442), Siena seizure detection (macro F1 0.622) and Bonn seizure detection (AUROC 0.999), had the highest accuracy of the seven compared models on TUEP epilepsy diagnosis (0.640) and, after fine-tuning, the highest \k{appa} (0.635) and weighted F1 (0.814) on TUEV event classification. It was the best of five models on P300 detection in autism with an unseen eight-electrode montage (AUROC 0.718). With only 5 of 19 electrodes, its mean AUROC fell only from 0.942 to 0.891. Conclusion. Identifying electrodes by position and modelling time without patches let one small model, pre-trained on one corpus, outperform much larger EEG foundation models on seizure detection, epileptiform event classification, epilepsy diagnosis and motor imagery.

ai.reason: Small, montage- and length-agnostic EEG foundation model with state-space layers; methodological ideas on channel-agnostic generalization are highly transferable.
ai.summary: Presents NOMAD-EEG, a 12.0M-parameter diffusion foundation model with state-space temporal layers and attention across electrodes identified by 3D scalp position, designed to be independent of montage, electrode count, and input length. Pre-trained on 147 h of unlabeled EEG, it outperformed seven foundation models on seizure detection, epilepsy diagnosis, and motor imagery tasks, with AUROC dropping only from 0.942 to 0.891 when using 5 of 19 electrodes.

papers.title: Accurate EEG-based linear state-space model of cortical dynamics during a passive motor task with exogenous input.
papers.abstract: Revealing the dynamics of the brain in the presence of exogenous inputs iscrucial for mechanistic understanding, interventions and regulations. We study state-spacemathematical modeling of brain's cortical dynamics using electroencephalography (EEG)data in an experiment with continuous exogenous input. We use subspaceidentification techniques to model the brain dynamics in a passive motor task experiment.The EEG data were recorded while participants were seated with their wrist strapped to ahaptic manipulator. The manipulator imposed a continuous multisine angularperturbation to the wrist as the exogenous input to the brain. Using twosubspace identification algorithms, we show that linear time-invariant state-space modelsaccurately represent the measurements, in a latent space, assuming that the EEG data arethe models' output. The model is verified and validated using data from sevenparticipants. Moreover, we construct linear maps to relate the latent space dynamics tothe neural source space. We verify that the findings of our model align with thoseidentified in previous studies. Accurate linear model in the presence ofexogenous input provides a pathway for designing parsimonious and simple controllers. Inaddition, it enables development of online monitoring, connectivity analysis and controlrelevant to neurorehabilitation, motor learning, and brain-computer interfacing.

ai.reason: Subspace-identification state-space modeling of EEG aligns strongly with the researcher's state-space and dynamical-system interest, though the task is motor rather than sleep.
ai.summary: Uses subspace identification to fit linear time-invariant state-space models of cortical dynamics from EEG during a passive motor task with continuous multisine wrist perturbation as exogenous input, validated across seven participants. Constructs linear maps relating latent dynamics to neural source space, with findings aligning with prior studies and supporting controller design and neurorehabilitation applications.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Acoustic Stimulation of Slow Oscillations Using a Wireless EEG Headband: A Polysomnography-Validated Feasibility Study.
papers.abstract: Acoustic stimulation precisely timed during sleep can enhance slow oscillations (SOs), a hallmark of deep sleep that is critical for restorative sleep. To date, this approach has largely been restricted to laboratory settings using high-density electroencephalography (EEG). Wearable EEG systems featuring closed-loop acoustic stimulation could enable scalable, home-based approaches to modulating slow-wave sleep. Here, we tested whether a real-time modeling approach (M-CLNS) could be implemented using a wireless EEG headband with forehead electrodes in healthy participants. Acoustic stimulation was delivered during a single night of sleep in alternating stimulation and sham conditions. We evaluated the accuracy of SO phase targeting utilizing the EEG headband and assessed whether it could be used to detect stimulation-induced changes in oscillatory dynamics. The findings were validated against simultaneous polysomnographic (PSG) recordings as an independent reference. We found that SO phase was targeted consistently near the intended phase using the headband, despite reduced amplitude and signal quality compared with simultaneous PSG. Acoustic stimulation produced an immediate enhancement of SO dynamics, as well as sustained increases in SO density and power spectral density within the SO and delta frequency range (0.75-5 Hz) during deep sleep. These effects were apparent both in the EEG headband and PSG signals. These results demonstrate the feasibility of closed-loop acoustic stimulation using a wireless EEG headband, providing a foundation for future home-based and clinical applications.

ai.reason: Sleep slow-oscillation stimulation with wearable EEG and PSG validation; relevant to sleep methodology and real-time signal quality handling.
ai.summary: Tested closed-loop acoustic stimulation of slow oscillations using a wireless EEG headband with forehead electrodes in healthy participants, validated against simultaneous polysomnography. Phase targeting was consistent near the intended phase, and stimulation produced immediate enhancement of slow oscillations plus sustained increases in SO density and power in the 0.75-5 Hz range during deep sleep.

papers.title: Dynamic Evolution of Quantitative Electroencephalography During Graded Intracranial Hypertension and Screening of Candidate Early-Warning Features in a Rabbit Model.
papers.abstract: Background and Objectives: Elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) is common to many encephalopathies, but the evolution of quantitative electroencephalography (qEEG) indices along a pressure gradient-and their relative suitability for early warning-have not been systematically compared. In this exploratory study we established a stepwise, steady-state rabbit model of graded intracranial hypertension and screened candidate early-warning features against prespecified criteria. Materials and Methods: Eight male New Zealand rabbits were studied; two were excluded-one for circulatory failure during catheterization and one for refractory status epilepticus that reached a humane endpoint-leaving six that completed the protocol. Repeated small-volume inflation of a left parenchymal water balloon was used to define five windows: baseline (BL; ICP < 10 mmHg), 15-20, 25-30 and 35-40 mmHg, and an end stage (END). Eight-channel EEG was recorded synchronously, and δ, θ, α and β power, together with the amplitude-integrated EEG (aEEG) upper margin, lower margin and bandwidth, were computed. Seven candidate features and three criteria (evolution timing, individual consistency and strength of association with ICP) were fixed before analysis; selection stability was assessed by leave-one-rabbit-out (LORO) cross-validation. Results: ICP rose in a controlled manner from 5.43 ± 1.09 to 35.93 ± 1.48 mmHg (Kendall W = 0.96), without systematic changes in respiratory mechanics. As ICP increased, absolute θ and α power declined progressively (ρ = -0.77 and -0.53), whereas absolute δ power did not increase and its rising relative share merely reflected redistribution after the loss of faster activity. The three aEEG components changed asynchronously: the lower margin shifted downward early and persistently (ρ = -0.87 with ICP; W = 0.86), whereas the upper margin changed only terminally and bandwidth showed no consistent direction. Concurrently, MAP rose through the Cushing response, with heart-rate slowing, but the rise was insufficient and CPP fell from 64.78 to 41.24 mmHg, approaching the rabbit lower limit of autoregulation (~50 mmHg CPP) only in the later windows. Because ICP and CPP were tightly coupled within animals, their independent effects on the EEG could not be separated. In leave-one-rabbit-out cross-validation, the lower margin was selected in five of six folds, with a median out-of-sample ρ of -1.00 (a discrete value based on four windows per animal). Conclusions: In this exploratory study in a small cohort (n = 6), qEEG indices evolved asynchronously along the ICP gradient; the aEEG lower margin appeared earliest and remained relatively stable across leave-one-rabbit-out folds, making it a candidate early-warning feature worthy of priority validation. However, because rising ICP and falling CPP were tightly coupled and could not be separated in this model, its early decline cannot be uniquely attributed to either ICP elevation or hypoperfusion. Its alarm threshold and early-warning value still require confirmation in larger independent cohorts with simultaneous CPP and cerebral blood flow monitoring.

ai.reason: Animal model with spectral qEEG and aEEG feature screening across states; transferable feature-engineering approach for animal neural time-series state analysis.
ai.summary: Established a stepwise graded intracranial hypertension model in rabbits to compare quantitative EEG indices along a pressure gradient and screen early-warning features. The amplitude-integrated EEG lower margin declined earliest and was selected in five of six leave-one-rabbit-out folds, while theta and alpha power fell progressively with rising ICP.

papers.title: Resting EEG as a condition-dependent ageing phenotype.
papers.abstract: Resting-state electroencephalography is increasingly proposed as a scalable marker of healthy brain ageing, yet its interpretability depends on distinguishing stable individual characteristics from condition-dependent measurement effects. This secondary analysis of an open lifespan dataset examined periodic alpha activity, alpha-peak detectability, aperiodic spectral structure, short-term repeatability, and longitudinal change under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions before and after an extended cognitive battery. Eye state strongly organised both whether a posterior alpha peak could be detected and the values of periodic and aperiodic measures. Age-related trajectories were prominent for the aperiodic exponent and full-sample alpha activity, whereas evidence that age modified post-battery change was weak. Across follow-up, detectable alpha frequency and the aperiodic exponent showed mean decreases, while alpha power was comparatively stable. Level measures demonstrated moderate-to-high repeatability and rank-order stability, but post-battery and difference-in-differences change scores were considerably less reliable. The findings position resting EEG as a condition-dependent ageing phenotype rather than a unitary baseline. They further show that peak detection, recording context, attrition, and the reliability of change must be modelled explicitly when resting EEG is used for lifespan inference or normative applications.

ai.reason: Spectral/aperiodic analysis and repeatability under condition changes; useful methodological caution for spectral feature reliability, adjacent to core interests.
ai.summary: Secondary analysis of an open lifespan resting-state EEG dataset examining alpha activity, peak detectability, aperiodic spectral structure, repeatability, and longitudinal change across eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions. Eye state strongly determined alpha peak detection and periodic/aperiodic measures, and change scores were considerably less reliable than level measures, positioning resting EEG as a condition-dependent ageing phenotype.

papers.title: FPGLNet: A Lightweight Frequency Prior-Gated Network for EEG Emotion Recognition.
papers.abstract: Although deep learning-based electroencephalography (EEG) emotion recognition methods have achieved promising performance, they generally depend on complex network architectures and high computational costs, which limits their deployment in resource-constrained scenarios. Meanwhile, existing approaches mainly focus on local spatiotemporal feature extraction while insufficiently exploiting global frequency-domain dependencies and dynamic information selection during feature propagation, resulting in inadequate spectral information utilization and redundant feature representations. To address these issues, this paper proposes a Frequency Prior-Gated Lightweight Network (FPGLNet) for EEG emotion recognition. First, a Mixed Aggregation Convolution (MAC) module is introduced at the input stage to jointly encode EEG spatiotemporal characteristics through temporal and spatial convolutions. Subsequently, a Fused Fourier Convolution Mixer (FFCM) module is developed to model global frequency-domain dependencies through Fourier transform and integrate multi-scale depthwise convolutions for collaborative frequency-spatial feature representation. Furthermore, a Prior-Gated Feed Forward Network (PGFN) is proposed to dynamically generate prior-guided gating weights based on feature responses, enabling adaptive selection and recalibration of discriminative features across different brain regions and temporal segments. This mechanism enhances emotion-related representations while suppressing noise and redundant information. Owing to the lightweight architecture design, FPGLNet achieves an effective balance between feature representation capability, model complexity, and computational efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that FPGLNet achieves classification accuracies of 96.22% and 92.69% on the public SEED-IV and SEED-V datasets, respectively. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed frequency prior-gated strategy in improving EEG feature representation while maintaining competitive recognition performance and deployment efficiency.

papers.title: How well does electrical source imaging reconstruct neural time series? Evidence from simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings
papers.abstract: Electrical source imaging (ESI) estimates neural activity from scalp EEG, but its ability to reconstruct the temporal dynamics of spontaneous brain activity beyond source localization remains unclear. This is assessed using simultaneous high-density EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG) recordings during spontaneous activity in 34 patients with drug-resistant focal epilepsy. Four ESI approaches (three distributed source models and one beamformer) are applied to estimate neural activity, which is then projected onto iEEG electrode locations to generate virtual iEEG signals for comparison with measured recordings. Reconstruction fidelity is quantified using Pearson correlations between actual and virtual iEEG signals, while spatial accuracy is assessed through peak localization error and spatial deviation derived from point-spread and cross-talk functions. Analyses are performed in broadband and delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Temporal reconstruction remains limited, with the highest estimated correlation reaching 0.126, localization errors of approximately 3 cm, and substantial spatial leakage. Reconstruction quality decreases with electrode depth and increasing frequency, while improving with higher epileptic spike rates. No single method is optimal across all metrics, although beamforming shows the weakest temporal reconstruction. These findings indicate that ESI only partially captures spontaneous intracranial dynamics and define spatial and temporal constraints for interpreting EEG-based source reconstructions.

papers.title: Ketones and Sleep: A Narrative Review of Mechanisms, Preclinical Models, and Human Evidence.
papers.abstract: Sleep is a metabolically dynamic state, and ketone bodies may interact with sleep physiology as both oxidative substrates and signaling metabolites. β-Hydroxybutyrate (BHB), acetoacetate (AcAc), and acetone rise during fasting, carbohydrate restriction, ketogenic diets used for therapeutic or non-therapeutic purposes, prolonged exercise, selected pathological states of insulin deficiency, and after consumption of exogenous ketones. This narrative review synthesizes mechanistic, preclinical, and human evidence linking endogenously generated ketosis and ketosis generated from exogenous ketone consumption to sleep architecture, sleep quality, sleep-disordered breathing, and sleep-relevant metabolic pathways. We reviewed studies involving ketogenic diets, fasting or caloric restriction, and consumption of exogenous ketones, prioritizing investigations with polysomnography, electroencephalography (EEG), sleep architecture, respiratory, or validated sleep-questionnaire outcomes, while also considering mechanistic studies of neuronal excitability, inflammation, epigenetic regulation, circadian timing, and brain energetics. The most direct preclinical evidence indicates that AcAc, but not BHB, increases slow-wave activity (delta power 0.5-4 Hz) during non-rapid eye movement (NREM) sleep and suppresses glutamate release in mice, supporting a potential role for ketone metabolism in sleep homeostasis. Dietary, fasting, and aging models further suggest that lipid/ketone metabolism can alter NREM/rapid eye movement (REM) balance, circadian metabolic rhythms, and sleep-wake responses to energetic stress, with aged-rat data showing sex-specific REM and cognitive effects of ketogenic interventions. Human studies are suggestive but heterogeneous: acute carbohydrate restriction can increase slow-wave sleep and reduce REM sleep in healthy adults; ketogenic therapies may improve subjective sleep in selected neurological and metabolic populations; and ketone ester ingestion can improve sleep efficiency after strenuous evening exercise, but not during hypoxia-induced sleep disruption. Ketones are sleep-relevant metabolic signals, but their effects are conditional rather than universally sleep-promoting. They may also indirectly affect sleep by enhancing wakefulness quality. The ketone concentration range associated with optimal sleep outcomes remains undefined, and potential dose-, timing-, and context-dependent effects on sleep require further study. Future studies should distinguish AcAc from BHB biology, measure nocturnal ketone dynamics, incorporate PSG/EEG spectral endpoints, and separate ketosis-specific effects from weight loss, energy deficit, exercise load, respiratory physiology, circadian timing, and disease-related confounders.

papers.title: REFS: Robust EEG feature selection with incomplete labels for multi-dimensional emotion recognition.
papers.abstract: Compared to single-type features, multi-type electroencephalography (EEG) features provide a multi-level representation for analyzing multi-dimensional emotions. However, the high dimensionality of multi-type EEG features, combined with the relatively small number of high-quality EEG samples, poses challenges such as classifier overfitting and suboptimal real-time performance in the multi-dimensional emotion recognition task. As the number of EEG channels increases, the issue will become increasingly severe. Moreover, practical applications of affective brain-computer interface frequently encounters partial absence of multi-dimensional emotional label data due to diverse emotional self-assessment models, and ambiguity and variability in individual emotion perception. To address these challenges, this study proposes a novel robust EEG feature selection method for incomplete multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The method leverages adaptive orthogonal latent semantic indexing to reconstruct the multi-dimensional emotional label space through second-order and higher-order relations, which could reduce the negative impact of missing values and outliers on label reconstruction. Simultaneously, it employs least squares regression with graph-based manifold learning regularization and global feature redundancy minimization regularization to enable EEG feature subset selection despite missing information, ultimately achieving robust and fast EEG-based multi-dimensional emotion recognition. The proposed method was validated on three multi-dimensional emotional datasets with varying channel configurations, namely DREAMER, DEAP and HDED, under different label missing ratios. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms thirteen state-of-the-art feature selection methods in terms of robustness for EEG emotional feature selection across various missing ratios. The proposed method provides a robust and efficient solution for feature selection in multi-dimensional emotion recognition under incomplete EEG label scenarios, delivering reliable performance for practical affective brain-computer interface applications.

papers.title: A Knowledge Transfer Method from Multi-Channel to Single-Channel EEG Toward Real-World Emotion Recognition Deployment.
papers.abstract: Multi-channel electroencephalography (EEG) provides spatial information for emotion recognition but requires more complex signal acquisition than single-channel EEG. This study proposes a multi-channel-to-single-channel knowledge transfer framework that uses multi-channel recordings during training and one selected physical EEG channel at inference. A 32-channel teacher is pretrained, and Sparsemax-based gating is jointly optimized with a student using classification, logits distillation, frequency-band consistency, and gating regularization losses. The frequency-band objective compares signal-level spectral statistics of the multi-channel recordings and the gated surrogate input. After channel locking, the student is retrained on the selected physical signal. Binary Arousal and Valence classification was evaluated on DEAP using 32-fold leave-one-subject-out cross-validation. The proposed achieved higher subject-averaged balanced accuracy and F1-score than Channel-matched CE in both tasks, although component effects varied across tasks and metrics. These findings support the evaluated training approach under single-channel input constraints and provide a methodological basis for simplifying EEG acquisition.

papers.title: Selection of Low-Density EEG Montages for Optimal Seizure Detection Performance.
papers.abstract: Multi-channel electroencephalography (EEG) is widely recognised for its ability to non-invasively capture dynamic brain activity with high temporal resolution. However, conventional EEG systems require meticulous setup, expert interpretation and specialised infrastructure, which limits their applicability in real-time, resource-constrained environments such as critical care and emergency settings. As wearable and point-of-care EEG technologies gain traction, there is increasing demand for low-density, automated seizure detection methods that are clinically reliable and scalable. This study presents a data-driven pipeline for an EEG-based task, seizure detection, that identifies compact and clinically relevant four-channel electrode configurations. Using standard 10-20 EEG recordings, the pipeline integrates clinical domain knowledge, preprocessing, feature extraction, and ensemble boosted classification to evaluate seizure detection performance across multiple electrode combinations. The approach was validated on both a heterogeneous local paediatric EEG dataset and an open-source adult dataset. Our results show that several four-channel montages achieve robust patient-independent performance, with central and temporal electrodes frequently appearing in the top-performing configurations. These findings support the feasibility of accurate seizure detection using low-density EEG, even across diverse clinical populations. The primary contribution of this work is a generalisable pipeline for selecting compact EEG montages, which balances domain insight and data-driven optimisation. This framework can be readily adapted to other EEG-based tasks and offers a practical path toward real-time wearable EEG monitoring in resource-constrained environments.

papers.title: [Multi-scale motor imagery electroencephalogram classification framework with dynamic weighted multi-source domain alignment].
papers.abstract: Brain-computer interface (BCI) technology facilitates information exchange between the brain and external devices, offering new approaches to human-computer interaction and medical rehabilitation. However, distribution shifts caused by inter-subject variability in electroencephalogram (EEG) signals limit classification performance and generalization. To address this issue, DWDANet, an EEG classification framework integrating multi-scale spatiotemporal feature modeling with dynamically weighted domain alignment, is developed. Multi-scale convolutions extracted spatiotemporal features, while a Transformer encoder modeled global dependencies. Multi-source domain alignment with dynamic weighting enhanced collaborative modeling across source domains and improved generalization. In within-subject evaluations, DWDANet achieved accuracies of 87.22%, 90.32%, and 68.82% on the BCI IV-2a, BCI IV-2b, and SHU-MI datasets, respectively. In cross-subject experiments, it achieved accuracies of 70.61%, 81.43%, and 64.38% on these datasets, respectively, outperforming other existing methods on all three. These results indicate that DWDANet could provide an effective approach to improving motor imagery EEG classification performance and cross-subject generalization.

papers.title: STDR-Net: A Spatio-Temporal Dependency Refinement Network for Motor Imagery EEG Decoding.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Motor imagery electroencephalography (MI-EEG) contains weak, non-stationary patterns that evolve across channels and time. Effective decoding requires local sensorimotor structure, trial-wide context, and ordered temporal evolution to be represented without discarding information from earlier processing stages. Methods: We propose STDR-Net, a Spatio-Temporal Dependency Refinement Network that recalibrates convolutional tokens, models their global interactions, restores the original local representation through a cross-stage residual bridge, and refines the fused sequence with a bidirectional long short-term memory network. STDR-Net was evaluated on BCI Competition IV-2a, BCI Competition IV-2b, and the PhysioNet EEG Motor Movement/Imagery dataset against nine reproduced baselines. The PhysioNet experiment used a pooled mixed-participant trial-level split rather than an unseen-participant evaluation. Results: STDR-Net obtained accuracies of 82.69%, 86.99%, and 59.76% and Cohen's kappa values of 0.7692, 0.7398, and 0.46, respectively. It achieved the highest observed mean accuracy on IV-2a and competitive performance on IV-2b and PhysioNet. Bridge-specific, ordering, module, and augmentation ablations supported the proposed pathway on IV-2a, whereas the differences on IV-2b were small and not significant after multiplicity correction. Conclusions: The results support information-preserving dependency refinement as a competitive design for MI-EEG decoding, while also showing that its benefit depends on the dataset and evaluation setting.

papers.title: EEG-guided robotic control of transcranial magnetic stimulation
papers.abstract: Brain-state-guided and closed-loop transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) protocols have emerged as methods for decreasing the outcome variability and increasing the therapeutic effectiveness of stimulation protocols. However, existing brain-state-dependent TMS systems control only stimulation timing, while the location is fixed and manually adjusted between blocks or sessions. This limits targeting distributed cortical networks in a flexible brain-state-dependent paradigm. We developed a method that jointly manages TMS pulse timing and location automatically controlled by electroencephalography (EEG)-derived brain state. A machine-learning algorithm infers the brain state in real time to guide robotic coil placement. We present a proof-of-concept study in which EEG controlled both the target site and the timing of TMS. A pre-trained convolutional neural network discriminated between resting state and movements performed with the right or left hand; the classifier output determined the hemisphere in which primary-motor-cortex hand area was stimulated. Preprocessing and decoding of 2-s EEG segments required 150 ms, and the robot took 7.5 s to move from the vertex home position to the predefined motor targets. The EEG-guided robotic TMS method expands the toolkit for brain-state-dependent neurostimulation by enabling closed-loop control of stimulus location based on EEG-derived brain states, including volitional activity. Thus, the method can benefit both neuroscience research and clinical neuromodulation applications, such as by optimizing stimulation parameters to the brain state that produces optimal rehabilitation outcomes in spinal cord injury or motor disorders.

papers.title: Beyond Modeling Order: Dual-Path Spatiotemporal Representation Learning for Cross-Subject EEG Emotion Recognition
papers.abstract: Cross-subject generalization remains a major challenge for EEG-based emotion recognition due to pronounced inter-subject variability in neural activity and emotion-related spatiotemporal patterns. Existing methods mainly alleviate inter subject differences through distribution alignment or contrastive learning, while paying limited attention to representation bias associated with fixed spatiotemporal modeling orders. We hypothesize that high-level emotion representations of the same EEG signal should remain consistent across different spatiotemporal modeling paths. Based on this hypothesis, we propose a Dual-Path Spatiotemporal Contrastive Learning (DP-STCL) framework for cross-subject EEG emotion recognition. DP-STCL employs two complementary encoders with independent parameters, namely a Temporal-to-Spatial (TS) path and a Spatial to-Temporal (ST) path, to model EEG spatiotemporal information under different integration orders. During representation learning, the same emotional stimulus is used to establish cross subject associations, while three complementary relations jointly constrain representation variations across subjects and modeling paths. This promotes stable and discriminative stimulus-related emotion representations. To further handle limited labeled target subject data, we introduce a LoRA-based few-shot adaptation strategy with low parameter overhead. Extensive cross-subject experiments on SEED, SEED-IV, SEED-V, and FACED show that DP-STCL consistently outperforms the compared methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in improving cross-subject EEG emotion recognition.

papers.title: OneEEG: A Unified Signal-Visual Multimodal Language Model with Task-Aware Mixture of Projectors for Multi-Task EEG Understanding
papers.abstract: Electroencephalography (EEG) is widely used in clinical assessment, brain-computer interfaces, and cognitive-state analysis, yet EEG modeling remains fragmented across task paradigms. Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) provide a promising interface for flexible multimodal reasoning, but their ability to understand EEG inputs remains limited. In this work, we propose OneEEG, a unified EEG-MLLM framework for multi-task EEG understanding. By training on our curated OneEEG-Instruct, a multi-task EEG instruction-tuning dataset, OneEEG jointly models numerical EEG representations and visual EEG representations, and introduces a task-aware Mixture of Projectors (MoP) to align heterogeneous EEG features across different task families with the LLM embedding space. We further establish OneEEG-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating current MLLMs and our method on multi-task EEG understanding. Experiments show that existing MLLMs have limited ability to interpret EEG inputs, while OneEEG achieves stronger performance by integrating numerical and visual EEG representations with task-aware EEG-to-LLM projection. Extensive ablations and analyses further reveal the effects of visual EEG renderings, MoP variants, router behavior, and feature dispersion across EEG tasks.

papers.title: MTFNet: A Lightweight Multi-Scale Time-Frequency Neural Network for Multi-Class Event Recognition in DAS-Based Perimeter Security.
papers.abstract: Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) has emerged as a pivotal technology for perimeter security. However, existing DAS event recognition methods have inherent limitations. Single-domain modeling has limited feature representation, while conventional multi-domain fusion methods require converting one-dimensional signals into two-dimensional images. This conversion adds computational overhead and may discard part of the original phase and amplitude information. In addition, the robustness of lightweight recognizers under low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) conditions remains insufficiently examined. This paper proposes a lightweight multi-scale time-frequency network (MTFNet) for direct processing of one-dimensional DAS signals. The model adopts a parallel time-frequency dual-branch architecture. The time-domain branch utilizes a lightweight 1D Inception-ResNet variant to capture short-term impulse features and long-range temporal dependencies via multi-scale parallel convolutions and residual connections. The frequency-domain branch performs multi-scale segmented spectral analysis to extract complementary discriminative information at diverse time and frequency resolutions, followed by a lightweight attention-free fusion module for effective time-frequency feature fusion. Experimental results on a self-built dataset covering Wind, Facility Noise, Hammering, Sawing, and Walking events show that MTFNet achieves a recognition accuracy of 99.55% with 0.12 M parameters, outperforming SVM, 1D-CNN, TCN, MS 1D-CNN, CNN-BiLSTM, and attention-based multimodal fusion methods. It maintains an accuracy of 94.06% at an SNR of 0 dB, demonstrating its robustness against additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) and practical engineering application potential.

papers.title: EEG-Based Machine Learning Classification of Shooting Conditions and Performance Levels During the Shooting Preparation Stage.
papers.abstract: Background: Shooting performance depends on environmental conditions and neural state during preparation. Few studies have applied machine learning (ML) to classify shooting conditions and performance levels using EEG. This study assessed whether pre-shot EEG features could discriminate shooting conditions and performance levels within the same condition. Methods: EEG and behavioral data from 35 shooters were analyzed under normal, noise, and low-light conditions. Band-power, phase-locking value (PLV)-based functional-connectivity, and filter bank common spatial pattern (FBCSP) features were evaluated separately using support vector machine (SVM) and random forest (RF). EEGNet served as an end-to-end benchmark for performance classification. Repeated trial-wise five-fold cross-validation assessed within-dataset trial-level discrimination, while supplementary leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV) assessed generalization to unseen shooters in the performance task. Results: All three feature types provided discriminative information for shooting conditions and high- versus low-performance trials. FBCSP combined with SVM achieved the best within-dataset performance, reaching 91% for normal versus low-light classification and 81% for high versus low performance under the normal condition. Because trials from the same participants could occur in both training and test folds, these accuracies were not estimates of subject-independent performance. LOSO-CV accuracies ranged from 59% to 70%, indicating limited cross-subject generalization. Beta-band features showed relatively consistent discriminative contributions. Gamma-band and frontal-channel findings require caution because residual muscle activity and attenuation of frontal EEG during virtual-EOG-based correction could not be excluded. Conclusions: Pre-shot EEG features showed preliminary within-dataset discriminability, but inter-individual variability limited generalization. Larger independent datasets, dedicated EOG/EMG recordings, and subject-adaptation strategies are required before practical deployment.

papers.title: EEG Features of Cortical Intent for Urination and Defecation in Healthy Aging and Spinal Cord Injury: A Descriptive Feasibility Study for BCI Neurorehabilitation.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Systematically elucidating the neural mechanisms of bowel and bladder control is crucial for developing closed-loop brain-computer interface (BCI) neurorehabilitation for patients with spinal cord injury (SCI). This study aims to characterize the spatiotemporal Electroencephalography (EEG) dynamics and compensatory cortical reorganization underlying continence motor intentions across healthy aging and SCI cohorts. Methods: 32-channel EEG signals were collected from healthy young adults, healthy older adults, and SCI patients during motor attempt paradigms of suppressed urination and defecation (SUD) and active urination and defecation (UD). Data were analyzed utilizing event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) and phase-locking value (PLV) functional connectivity across alpha (8-13 Hz), beta1 (13-20 Hz), and beta2 (20-30 Hz) bands. Results: All cohorts exhibited generally consistent broadband event-related desynchronization (ERD) in the sensorimotor cortex (SMC) during visceral motor attempt. Conversely, the frontal cortex (FC) demonstrated marked frequency-band differentiation. During the SUD task, healthy older adults showed significantly greater SMC beta2 ERD than young adults, whereas SCI patients showed a similar but non-significant trend. Frontal beta2 findings were preliminary and should be interpreted with caution due to potential residual artifacts. Network analysis revealed that physiological aging and SCI are associated with large-scale topological reconfigurations, prominently featuring enhanced long-range frontal functional connectivity to compensate for sensory or peripheral deficits. Conclusions: High-level cortical intentions for continence are preserved after SCI, with frontal high-frequency activity possibly reflecting a compensatory process for sensorimotor disruption. These findings substantiate that visceral intentions exhibit discernible characteristics at the cortical level, establishing a spatiotemporal framework for targeted pelvic nerve modulation via brain-machine interfaces.

papers.title: Association Between EEG Activity and Motor Imagery Ability in Single-Joint Movements: A Pilot Study.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: This exploratory pilot study examined whether motor imagery ability is associated with electroencephalography (EEG) oscillatory activity during single-joint motor imagery. Methods: Eleven healthy young adults performed motor execution, kinesthetic motor imagery (KMI), and visual motor imagery (VMI) of right wrist dorsiflexion. Motor imagery ability was assessed using the Kinesthetic and Visual Imagery Questionnaire (KVIQ). Time-frequency EEG data were analyzed using cluster-based permutation tests. Based on the study hypotheses, kinesthetic KVIQ scores were examined in relation to task-onset-locked KMI activity, and visual KVIQ scores were examined in relation to task-offset-locked VMI activity. A Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of p < 0.025 was applied across the two analyses. Results: No condition-level EEG differences were observed among motor execution, KMI, and VMI. Kinesthetic KVIQ scores were negatively associated with 6.5-13 Hz activity at O1 during KMI (p = 0.024), whereas visual KVIQ scores were positively associated with post-task 10-16.5 Hz activity at F7 during VMI (p = 0.023). Both met the Bonferroni-adjusted significance threshold. The corresponding descriptive Pearson correlations were r = -0.869 and r = 0.937. Conclusions: These exploratory findings should not be interpreted as confirmatory evidence of stable brain-behavior associations; the reported correlations are descriptive summaries based on clusters selected from the same dataset. Replication in a larger, independent study with prespecified analyses and objective measures of imagery performance is needed.

In addition, EEGNet achieved the highest mean accuracy (84.06±15.57%), followed by SVM (81.56±14.23%) and LDA (76.56±15.30%).

papers.title: Wave-function formalism for evolving neural dynamics: a mathematical framework informed by EEG.
papers.abstract: The organization of distributed neural activity remains one of the central challenges in computational neuroscience. Contemporary frameworks, including Integrated Information Theory, Global Workspace Theory, entropy-based approaches, and electromagnetic field theories, have advanced our understanding of neural coordination but employ different mathematical descriptions of large-scale brain dynamics. This study investigates whether wave-function formalism provides a useful mathematical framework for representing evolving neural dynamics measured using electroencephalography (EEG). Rather than introducing a new electrophysiological measure or proposing a new mechanism of consciousness, the framework represents complementary EEG observables within a common state-space description of neural activity. Mathematical inspiration is drawn from Everett's representation of evolving state spaces, although no claims are made regarding quantum computation or quantum processes in the brain. Electroencephalographic recordings from interictal, preictal, and ictal seizure states (150 EEG segments) were analyzed using complementary measures of signal amplitude, spectral organization, entropy, phase dynamics, cross-frequency coupling, and recurrence quantification. Statistical comparisons employed nonparametric analyses, effect-size estimation, confidence intervals, and post hoc testing. Significant differences were observed across all major electrophysiological domains. Ictal recordings exhibited increased signal amplitude, redistribution of spectral power toward lower frequencies, reduced entropy, altered phase organization, changes in cross-frequency coupling, and increased recurrence structure, indicating coordinated changes in evolving neural dynamics during seizure progression. These findings are interpreted within a mathematical framework that treats established EEG observables as complementary descriptors of a single evolving neural state. The principal contribution of this work is the proposal of a mathematically grounded and experimentally testable representation of evolving neural dynamics. Whether this formalism provides new insight into cognition or conscious experience remains an empirical question for future investigation.

papers.title: Procalcitonin and C-Reactive Protein Are Elevated at the Threshold of Cortical Electrocerebral Silence but Do Not Track Graded EEG Severity in Critically Ill Children: A Single-Centre Retrospective Cohort Study.
papers.abstract: The relationship between routine inflammatory biomarkers and EEG severity in critically ill children, evaluated using visual (Synek) grading and spectral qEEG, remains unclear. The aim of our study was to examine the associations between procalcitonin (PCT), C-reactive protein (CRP) and EEG severity. Single-centre retrospective cohort of 97 critically ill children were analysed (PICU, Romania; November 2022-February 2026), each contributing one EEG with an inflammatory biomarker measured within ≤24 h. The primary analysis was the Spearman correlation of PCT and CRP with Synek grade, supported by comparisons of cortical electrocerebral silence with preserved cortical activity (Synek 1-4). The secondary analysis comprised five age-adjusted partial Spearman correlations between biomarkers and spectral qEEG metrics in the spectral cohort (n = 71), BH-corrected within family. PCT and CRP were markedly higher in cortical silence than in preserved activity (Mann-Whitney p-value = 9.6 × 10-6 and 4.1 × 10-6; adjusted OR ≈ 2 per ln-unit). Both markers showed a positive rank association across Synek grades (PCT ρ = +0.49; CRP ρ = +0.41; both BH-adjusted p-value < 10-4), driven by the Synek-5 step: within grades 1-4 neither was graded (PCT ρ = +0.19; CRP ρ = +0.08; both p-value > 0.1). None of the five secondary correlations suggested a moderate-to-strong association (ρ -0.14 to +0.08; all BH-adjusted p-value ≥ 0.668). PCT and CRP were elevated at the threshold of cortical electrocerebral silence but did not provide a graded severity index within Synek grades 1-4, nor did they associate with spectral qEEG, including in the full 10-20 subset. The spectral analysis was underpowered for weak effects and excluded the Synek-5 subset where the primary signal was localised.

papers.title: Multimodal Neurorehabilitation Including Auditory EEG Neurofeedback: A Proof of Concept Tested After Resection of a Giant Olfactory Groove Meningioma.
papers.abstract: Background/Objectives: Patients undergoing resection of large olfactory groove meningiomas may present with persistent cognitive, behavioral, motor, and functional impairments. Evidence regarding EEG neurofeedback as part of postoperative neurorehabilitation remains preliminary. This case report describes the feasibility and associated clinical and neurophysiological changes in a sensory-adapted multimodal rehabilitation program. Methods: A 53-year-old man underwent emergency resection of a giant olfactory groove meningioma and subsequently completed 20 inpatient rehabilitation sessions over four weeks. Each session included auditory SMR/theta EEG neurofeedback at Cz, individualized cognitive training, and physiotherapy. Neuropsychological, emotional, functional, and mobility outcomes were assessed before and after treatment. EEG outcomes included longitudinal single-channel recordings acquired during neurofeedback sessions and 19-channel resting-state recordings obtained under eyes-open and eyes-closed conditions before and after the program. Spectral power, spectral ratios, and weighted phase-lag index connectivity were analyzed descriptively. Results: Reliable or measurement-based improvements were observed in global cognition, executive functioning, immediate and delayed verbal recall, total and cognitive functional independence, and mobility. Across the 20 neurofeedback sessions, the conservative primary analysis retained 9936 of 10,261 epochs and showed reduced theta activity, increased SMR and beta activity, increased SMR/theta, and reduced theta/total-beta. Resting-state EEG showed lower relative theta power and higher SMR, beta-1, and beta-2 power under both recording conditions. Connectivity changes included reduced theta and posterior alpha coupling together with increased SMR connectivity across fronto-central and parieto-occipital networks. Conclusions: Sensory-adapted EEG neurofeedback was feasible within an intensive multimodal rehabilitation program and was accompanied by concurrent cognitive, functional, and neurophysiological changes. Because of the single-case, uncontrolled, multimodal design, the findings cannot establish treatment-specific efficacy and should be considered hypothesis-generating.

papers.title: Eye movement and EEG features in generalized anxiety disorder.
papers.abstract: Generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) is a common psychiatric condition that severely impacts individuals' mental health and quality of life. However, its diagnosis and treatment remain challenging in clinical practice, largely relying on subjective assessments and lacking objective, quantitative biological markers. Therefore, this study aimed to compare eye movement and electroencephalography (EEG) features between GAD patients and healthy controls, and to evaluate the classification performance of eye movement, EEG, and their combined features using machine learning. Twenty-nine GAD patients and 27 healthy controls were recruited. Clinical symptoms, cognitive function, eye movement, and EEG data were collected. Descriptive statistics and partial correlation analyses were conducted to compare group differences and explore feature associations. A linear support vector machine (SVM) model was constructed using eye movement, EEG, and combined features for classification. GAD patients exhibited eye movement abnormalities, including reduced fixation duration, increased saccade velocity, enlarged vertical saccade amplitude, and prolonged antisaccade latency, as well as abnormal beta power during Go/Nogo tasks. The model combining eye movement and EEG features achieved the best overall performance, outperforming models based on eye movement or EEG features alone. The relatively small sample size warrants further validation in larger cohorts. Multimodal neurophysiological features integrating eye movement and EEG improve classification performance for GAD and may serve as potential objective biomarkers.

papers.title: Network-Resolved and Frequency-Specific EEG-fMRI Representational Similarity Analysis of Visual Imagery.
papers.abstract: Background: Visual imagery (VI) is a cognitive process that generates visual representations in the absence of external visual input; however, the spatiotemporal organization of its neural representations remains poorly understood. Methods: In this study, we combined electroencephalography (EEG) and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) with representational similarity analysis (RSA) and the Schaefer 2018 functional parcellation atlas to compare the correspondence between brain network representations and CORnet-S model representations during visual perception (VP) and VI. We further examined the cross-modal associations between EEG time-frequency representations and fMRI network representations during VI. Results: Significant model-brain representational correspondence was detected in the visual network during VP, and no significant correspondence was detected in any network during VI, yielding different descriptive significance profiles across the two tasks. Cross-modal EEG-fMRI RSA further revealed frequency- and time-dependent representational correspondence involving the frontoparietal, default mode, ventral attention, visual, and limbic networks. Significant cross-modal correspondence was observed across the alpha, beta, and gamma bands, with descriptive variation in the networks and temporal clusters involved in each frequency band. Conclusions: Collectively, these findings suggest that VI is not merely a reinstatement of VP but is associated with distributed representational patterns involving multiple functional networks. This study provides multimodal evidence for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying VI.

papers.title: Early Post-Operative Quantitative EEG Central Beta Power Predicts Futile Recanalization After Endovascular Treatment in AIS-LVO.
papers.abstract: Despite successful endovascular recanalization in acute ischemic stroke, approximately 50%-55% of patients experience 90-day futile recanalization (FR). We evaluated the prognostic value of central relative beta power derived from early postoperative quantitative electroencephalography (QEEG) and explored QEEG associations with brain edema and parenchymal hemorrhage. This retrospective, single-center subgroup analysis of the prospective multicenter DETECT2-China registry included 56 patients with acute ischemic stroke due to large-vessel occlusion. Patients underwent 20-30-min EEG recordings approximately 24 h after successful endovascular treatment. Multivariable logistic regression adjusting for seven clinical covariates, Firth and reduced-model sensitivity analyses, and leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) with the DeLong test were performed. An additional sensitivity analysis repeated QEEG feature selection within each training set. Feature reliability was evaluated using split-half intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). Of 56 patients, 31 (55.4%) developed 90-day FR. Higher central relative beta power was independently associated with lower odds of FR (adjusted OR: 0.28 per 1-SD increase, 95% CI: 0.11-0.74, p = 0.010). Integrating central beta power into the clinical model increased the fixed-feature LOOCV area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) from 0.557 to 0.719 (DeLong p = 0.007). In exploratory analyses, delta-band Brain Symmetry Index specifically tracked parenchymal hemorrhage (PH vs. no intracranial hemorrhage [No ICH], p = 0.006). Exploratory graph analysis also showed macro-scale network disintegration in FR patients. All QEEG features demonstrated high split-half reliability (ICC ≥ 0.75). Central relative beta power recorded approximately 24 h after endovascular treatment was independently associated with 90-day FR and showed potential incremental prognostic value. Exploratory associations with postoperative complications suggest that QEEG may provide a non-invasive bedside "brain window" for neurocritical care.

papers.title: Tablet-Camera Iris Landmarks and EEG/PPG-Derived Arousal Indices During Naturalistic Reading: Geometric Confounding and Exploratory Within-Subject Associations.
papers.abstract: Arousal, the activation dimension of the valence-arousal circumplex, indexes alertness and engagement independently of pleasantness. We evaluated whether MediaPipe FaceLandmarker iris landmark distances from a tablet camera estimate electroencephalography (EEG)- and photoplethysmography (PPG)-derived arousal markers during naturalistic reading. Recordings from 48 participants yielded 43,923 thirty-second windows. Raw iris distances correlated with EEG alpha (r=+0.118) and theta (r=+0.076), but face scale explained 93% of their variance. After face-width normalisation, alpha remained associated (r=+0.076), whereas theta was not statistically significant. Further adjustment for ocular luminance and head pose rendered alpha nonsignificant (r=+0.021, p=0.33). Circular-shift testing identified alpha coupling in 11/48 participants under full control, versus 28/48 using uncorrected Pearson tests. Within-subject Ridge regression, with no raw sample shared between the training and test windows, yielded a nonsignificant group mean correlation (r=+0.078, p=0.07); 13/48 participants had individually significant prediction-reference associations (11 positive), fewer when the PPG term was restricted to filter-consistent beats. Both counts are exploratory, nominal and uncorrected across participants, and come from different analyses. Neither establishes prospective monitoring performance, and the study does not validate the landmark distance as a pupil measure.

papers.title: Inhibition of miR-206 Ameliorates Seizures and Cognitive Deficits via BDNF/TrkB Signaling in Pilocarpine-Induced TLE Mice.
papers.abstract: Objectives: Temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) causes spontaneous seizures, hippocampal neuronal loss, and cognitive impairment. This study investigated whether miR-206 inhibition attenuates seizures and cognitive dysfunction by activating the BDNF/TrkB cascade in mice with pilocarpine-induced TLE. Methods: Fifty TLE-model C57BL/6N mice were divided into five groups. MiR-206 antagomir or a negative control was stereotaxically injected into the hippocampus. ANA-12, a TrkB inhibitor, was given intraperitoneally. We detected miR-206 with RT-qPCR. EEG was used to assess seizure activity. Spatial cognition was measured via the Morris water maze. Neuronal injury was evaluated using HE and Nissl staining. Target protein levels were quantified by Western blotting. Hippocampal miR-206 was elevated in TLE mice. Results: MiR-206 antagomir lowered miR-206 expression. It prolonged seizure latency. It reduced seizure frequency and duration. It restored spatial learning and memory function. It relieved CA3 neuronal loss and up-regulated BDNF/TrkB, SYP, and PSD95. ANA-12 abolished these protective phenotypes. Conclusions: MiR-206 inhibition confers anti-seizure, neuroprotective, and cognition-improving effects. These benefits depend on functional BDNF/TrkB signalling. miR-206 is a potential therapeutic target for TLE.

papers.title: From one risky choice to the next: Trait dominance, feedback, and response-locked EEG in corporate leaders.
papers.abstract: Repeated risky choice can reflect both the direction of choice and whether a previous choice is repeated, but these patterns are not always distinguished in research on trait dominance. In this secondary analysis, 28 male corporate leaders completed a repeated monetary gambling task with complete feedback while EEG was recorded. Mixed-effects models examined associations of trait dominance, choice history, and feedback with subsequent High-risk choice, Stay/Switch behavior, response time, and response-locked FCz activity. Higher dominance was associated with greater odds of choosing High after both previous High- and Low-risk choices, with no reliable difference between the two history-specific associations. In the direct transition model, a 1-SD increase in continuous dominance corresponded to 47% higher odds of Current High choice (OR = 1.47, 95% CI [1.25, 1.73]). On the Stay/Switch scale, higher dominance predicted staying after High but switching after Low, indicating a High-directed pattern rather than uniformly greater repetition of the preceding risk level. Recent outcomes also remained consequential: absolute valence and comparative favorability were associated with subsequent choice, and responses were 12.7% slower after Gains than Losses, whereas dominance was not reliably related to response time. EEG findings were more qualified: mean FCz voltage was more positive in the predefined High-dominance group, whereas peak latency showed a feedback-dependent dominance contrast between Gain-Correct and Gain-Error trials; no individual condition-specific dominance slope survived Holm correction. Trait dominance was therefore associated most clearly with the direction of repeated risky choice, while recent experience continued to shape the next decision.

papers.title: How Aesthetic and Economic Factors Affect Consumers' Purchasing Decisions: Evidence from EEG.
papers.abstract: Consumer theory identifies cultural and economic factors as key influences on purchasing decisions. Artworks, as material carriers of culture, are shaped by these factors in a particularly pronounced way. This study proposes that consumers' artwork purchasing decisions are jointly determined by aesthetic and economic considerations. Using event-related potential (ERP) technology, artworks were classified into a 2 by 2 matrix of aesthetic valence and price. Seventy students from a university in western China made purchase or rejection decisions while their electroencephalogram was recorded. Results showed that both aesthetic and price factors jointly influenced artwork purchasing decisions. Aesthetic valence had a larger effect (F(1, 69) = 134.98, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.662) than price (F(1, 69) = 22.47, p < 0.001, ηp2 = 0.246), and participants were most willing to buy positively rated, low-priced artworks (M = 42.2%, SD = 24.2). The medial frontal negativity (MFN) amplitude and theta-band power were larger during purchase than rejection decisions, and this difference was most pronounced when participants chose to buy negatively rated artworks (t(48) = 4.31, p < 0.001, d = 0.61). Because the sample was drawn from a single university in western China and consisted of young students, the conclusions carry generalisability limitations. This study maps aesthetic and economic considerations during consumer purchasing onto separable neural processes, contributing to the intersection of cultural neuroscience and neuroeconomics.
